I’m sixty, I’ve farmed these six mu for thirty years, and I finished senior high—so unlike some of my neighbors who go by bags and scoops, I read the fertilizer labels and calculate the N-P-K rates myself. With only six mu and three people in the household, every yuan matters, but a bad year hurts more than a slightly expensive input. I know this land: the soil is loamy, drains well, but it needs replenishment every season. My son works off-farm, so it’s mainly me and my wife handling the field, with hired labor only at harvest. I’m not experimenting this year—wheat-maize double cropping has been stable, and change is risky when the margin is thin.

For winter wheat, I’ll plant the full six mu in mid-October. I use improved wheat seed because the germination is reliable and the yield is proven. I do rotary tillage before sowing to break the stubble and level the seedbed. For fertilizer, I target about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu: a compound fertilizer base plus a urea topdressing at jointing. I also apply roughly 6 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium per mu, calculated from the compound bag ratios. Irrigation is costly because I pump from a tube well, but three times is the minimum for a safe wheat crop here—winter irrigation, one at jointing, and one at heading. I spray pesticides four times: a herbicide at early stage, then fungicide and insecticide as the season progresses. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 500 kg per mu.

For summer maize, the window between wheat harvest and maize planting is barely a week in mid-June, so I plant no-till like everyone else in the village—there’s no time to till. I use hybrid seed; the price is higher, but the yield response pays back easily. Maize gets about 16 kg nitrogen per mu, with similar phosphorus and potassium as the wheat. Summer rains usually help, so I plan two irrigations—one at the V6 stage and one at tasseling—unless the monsoon is exceptionally strong. Three pesticide applications are enough for maize. On a normal year, I expect around 550 kg per mu.
